lesson.title: What it really costs

lead.text: Take an afternoon with £20 to spend, where a paperback costs £8 and a bubble tea costs £4. Buy the book and the shop takes £8, which is the price on the label. The same £8 would have bought two teas, though, and once it has gone into the book it can't buy them. So the book has a second price, which is two bubble teas.

Economists call what you give up the opportunity cost of a choice. It is the value of the best alternative you passed over, and the word best matters. Suppose the £8 could also have gone on a magazine or a bus fare. You could only have taken one of them, so the cost of the book is whichever you would really have picked instead, and the others drop out.

Money isn't the only thing that runs out. Time works the same way, since an hour spent on one job is an hour another job can't have. That brings us to a workshop, where the price of one job is counted in the output of another.

lead.text: Now try the idea on a day's budget. Count the cost of the ticket in the thing you could have bought with the same money.

steps.headline: A week's work, priced in chairs

lead.text: Picture a joiner's workshop with one week to use. Workshop B can finish 40 chairs in a week, or 20 tables, if it makes nothing else. Both figures use the whole week, so they are two ways of spending the same time, and that lets us compare them.

Twenty tables take as long as 40 chairs, so one table takes as long as two chairs. Divide the chairs by the tables: 40 ÷ 20 = 2. A table's opportunity cost is 2 chairs, because 2 chairs are what the same time would have built. The rate also works the other way round, and a chair costs half a table.

afterFigure.text: The line in the picture joins the two extremes. The workshop swaps tables for chairs at one steady rate, so every extra table takes the same 2 chairs away. Another workshop with different weekly totals would swap at a different rate, and the next screen gives you one to price.

lead.text: Workshop A has its own week. It can build 60 chairs or 20 tables, and it swaps one for the other at a steady rate. Price a table in chairs, using the method from the last screen.

reveal.text: You just priced a table in chairs: 60 ÷ 20 = 3. That price, the chairs given up for each table, is its opportunity cost.

steps.headline: All the weeks a workshop could choose

lead.text: A workshop doesn't have to put the whole week into one good. Workshop B could give half its week to chairs and half to tables. Half a week of chairs is 20 chairs, and half a week of tables is 10 tables, so 20 chairs and 10 tables is a week it could build. Any other split of the week gives another pair of numbers in the same way.

afterFigure.text: Plot all of those pairs and they join into a line called the production possibilities frontier. It marks the edge of what the workshop can do with its time. On the line, every hour is used. Inside it, a mix such as 10 chairs and 5 tables leaves some hours idle. Beyond it, a mix would need more hours than the week has, so the workshop can't build it.
Each step along the frontier swaps one good for the other, so each step has an opportunity cost, and the next screens read those costs off the line.

cases.label: Workshop B, half a week each
Workshop C, half a week each

lead.text: Workshop A can build 60 chairs or 20 tables in a week at a steady rate. Check where one particular week falls against its frontier.

steps.headline: Pricing a step along a curved frontier

lead.text: So far the swap rate has been the same everywhere along the line. Many real frontiers curve. Take a country that makes food and machines. If it grows no food it can build 100 machines, and if it puts everything into farming it can grow 80 units of food and build none. Between those ends the frontier is a curve, drawn in the picture.

On a curve the price of food depends on where you stand, so we price it one short step at a time. Take the first step, from no food to 20 units. The machines drop from 100 to 90, so 10 machines are given up for 20 more units of food. Each unit of food costs 10 ÷ 20 = 0.5 machines.

afterFigure.text: The rule is the same as before, applied to a step: divide what you give up by what you gain. Next you will price a later step on the same frontier.

steps.headline: A country makes food and machines. Moving from 40 to 60 food, what does each extra unit of food cost?

workedSteps.text: Read the frontier. At 40 food it sits at 70 machines; at 60 food it sits at 40.
Share the loss across the gain.

lead.text: Price the next step along the same frontier. An average over the whole frontier would hide how the cost changes from one step to the next.

reveal.text: This step cost 2 machines per unit of food, and the step before it cost 1.5. The price of food is rising.

lead.text: Lay the four steps along the country's frontier side by side. They cost 0.5, 1, 1.5 and 2 machines for each extra unit of food, so the price of food keeps climbing as the country grows more of it. The steps from 20 to 40 and from 40 to 60 give 20 ÷ 20 = 1 and 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5, which fill in the middle.

The reason is that resources aren't equally good at both jobs. The first food comes from fertile land and from workers who did little in the factories, so few machines are lost. Later food has to pull engineers and factory sites onto the farms, and each unit of food then takes more machines with it.

afterFigure.text: A cost that rises like this is called increasing opportunity cost, and it gives the frontier its outward bow. If every resource suited both goods equally, the cost would stay the same at every step and the frontier would be a straight line, like the workshops'.

lead.text: Think about the shape of the country's frontier, a curve that bulges away from the origin.
Not every trade-off bends. Priya splits her study time between essays and problem sets, and each task takes a fixed time, so her trade-off is a straight line.

lesson.orientation: Measure opportunity cost along a production possibilities frontier, and see why it usually rises.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A joiner has one week and one workshop. She can spend the week building chairs or building tables, and a week only has so many hours. Every table she builds uses hours that would have gone into chairs, so a table's real price is the chairs she didn't make.

Your own Saturday works the same way. Money and time can each be spent once, and when you spend them on one thing you give up whatever else they would have bought. Anyone who plans how a business, a household or a whole country uses what it has needs a way of counting that hidden price.

This lesson starts with your own spending and then follows the joiner's week. We'll work out the price of a choice, draw every week she could pick, and watch what happens to the price as she asks more of the workshop.

intro.promise: By the end you'll price a choice by what it gives up, and read that price off a frontier.

recap.keyIdea: A choice costs the best alternative you give up. Along a frontier that cost is the machines lost per unit of food gained, and it usually rises.

blocks.text: Back at the joiner's week, a table now has a price in chairs. You counted a cinema ticket in sandwiches, a table at 3 chairs, and then food on a curved frontier, where the first step cost 0.5 machines a unit and the last cost 2.

recap.nextHook: Each workshop and each country has its own prices, and the next lesson sets two bakers side by side to see who should make what.

questions.prompt: Workshop A can make at most 60 chairs or 20 tables a week, trading one for the other at a constant rate. How many chairs does each extra table cost?
hints: Both maximums use the same week of work.
Ask how many chairs one table's share of the week could have made.
Divide the maximum number of chairs by the maximum number of tables.
questions.onCorrect: 3 chairs. A table's opportunity cost is the chairs the same slice of the week could have made: 60 ÷ 20.

misconceptions.feedback: 20 is the most tables the week allows. The question asks how many chairs one table replaces.
That is every chair the week could make. One table uses only its slice of the week.
The goods trade at a ratio, so subtracting the maximums does not work. Compare them by dividing.

questions.prompt: Workshop A can make at most 60 chairs or 20 tables a week at a constant rate. It makes 30 chairs and 5 tables. Where does that point lie?
hints: Work out how many tables the time left after 30 chairs could make.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Thirty chairs leave time for 10 tables, so 5 tables wastes capacity: the point is inside the frontier.

questions.onCorrect: Inside. 30 chairs use half the week, which could make 10 tables, so making 5 leaves time idle.

misconceptions.feedback: On the frontier means all the week is used. Work out how many tables the time left after 30 chairs could make.
Beyond the frontier needs more time than the week holds. Check how much of the week 30 chairs use.

questions.prompt: Machines given up in moving from 40 to 60 food
hints: Only the machines column matters for what is given up.
Find machines at both points.
Subtract the later figure from the earlier one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Machines fall from 70 to 40: 70 − 40 = 30 machines for 20 more food.

questions.onCorrect: Machines fall from 70 to 40, so 30 machines are given up for 20 more food.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the machines at the starting point. What is given up is the fall between the two points.
That is the machines at the end point. Take the change from start to end.
That is the food gained. The question asks about machines.

questions.prompt: On a country's bowed frontier, food rises from 60 to 80 units while machines fall from 40 to 0. What is the opportunity cost per unit of food, measured in machines?
hints: Find the machines lost on this step.
Find the food gained on this step.
Divide the loss by the gain.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 40 machines ÷ 20 food = 2 machines per unit of food.

questions.onCorrect: 2 machines per unit. The step from 60 to 80 food costs more per unit than the step before it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the machines lost in total. Divide by the food gained to price one unit.
That is the food gained, not the machines given up per unit.
That averages over the whole frontier. Use only the step from 60 to 80 food.

questions.prompt: Priya has 12 hours of study time. An essay takes her 3 hours and a problem set takes 1.5 hours. What is the opportunity cost of one essay, measured in problem sets?
hints: An essay uses up a fixed block of time.
Ask how many problem sets fit into that same block.
Divide the essay's time by the time for one problem set.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 ÷ 1.5 = 2 problem sets per essay. The 12-hour total does not change the rate.

questions.onCorrect: 2 problem sets. An essay's cost is the other task's output over the same time; the 12-hour total does not change the rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many essays 12 hours allow. Compare one essay's time with one problem set's time.
That is a problem set's cost in essays, the wrong way up.
That is every problem set 12 hours could hold. One essay uses only its own block of time.

questions.prompt: A production possibilities frontier bows outward from the origin. What does that shape show about the opportunity cost of the good on the horizontal axis?
hints: Compare how steep the frontier is near each axis.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each extra unit of one good costs more of the other, as resources less suited to it are moved across.

questions.onCorrect: Each extra unit of one good costs more of the other, because resources less suited to it are moved across.

misconceptions.feedback: A constant cost gives a straight line, not a bow.
Falling cost would bend the frontier inward, towards the origin.

questions.prompt: You have £30 for the day. A sandwich costs £5. You buy a £10 cinema ticket. How many sandwiches did the ticket cost you?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: £10 buys 10 ÷ 5 = 2 sandwiches, so the ticket cost 2 sandwiches.

hints: What could the £10 have bought instead?
Each sandwich is £5. How many fit into the ticket's price?
Divide the ticket price by the price of one sandwich.
questions.onCorrect: 2. The ticket's real price includes what the same money would have bought. That hidden price is what economists count.

misconceptions.feedback: That's every sandwich the £30 could buy. Only the £10 you spent on the ticket is in play.
That's how many tickets £30 buys. The question asks about sandwiches.

questions.prompt: Mia has a free hour and picks a film. Her next-best options were football, then revising. What is the film's opportunity cost?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Football. The cost is the best alternative given up, and she could only have done one thing instead.

hints: Which single option would she have chosen if not the film?
questions.onCorrect: Football. Only the best alternative counts: it is the one thing she would actually have done instead.

misconceptions.feedback: She had one hour, so she could not have done both. Only one alternative can be the cost.
Revising was her least favourite. The cost is the option she would most have wanted instead.

questions.prompt: Machines given up per unit of food

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 30 machines ÷ 20 food = 1.5 machines per unit of food.

hints: Use the machines given up and the food gained from the lines above.
Share the loss across the units of food you gain.
Divide the loss by the gain.
questions.onCorrect: 1.5. Divide what is given up by what is gained to price each unit of food.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total given up. Share it across the units of food gained.
That is the food gained. Divide the machines lost by it.

questions.prompt: A farm can grow 100 tonnes of wheat or 25 tonnes of barley with its land, at a constant rate. What is the opportunity cost of one tonne of barley, in tonnes of wheat?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 ÷ 25 = 4 tonnes of wheat per tonne of barley.

hints: One tonne of barley uses a share of the land. How much wheat could that share grow?
Compare the two maximums that use the same land.
Divide the wheat figure by the barley figure.
questions.onCorrect: 4 tonnes of wheat. Divide the wheat the land could grow by the barley it could grow.

misconceptions.feedback: That is wheat's cost in barley, the wrong way up.
The goods trade at a ratio, so subtracting does not work. Divide instead.

questions.prompt: A frontier passes through (10 food, 90 machines) and (25 food, 45 machines). What is the opportunity cost per unit of food between them, in machines?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Machines fall by 90 − 45 = 45 while food rises by 25 − 10 = 15, so 45 ÷ 15 = 3.

hints: Find how far machines fall between the two points.
Find how far food rises.
Divide the fall in machines by the rise in food.
questions.onCorrect: 3 machines per unit of food: the fall in machines divided by the rise in food.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total machines given up. Divide by the food gained.
That is the food gained, not the cost per unit.

questions.prompt: A café's frontier is bowed. Shifting the first 20 cups towards tea costs 10 cups of coffee. The next 20 cups of tea cost 25 cups of coffee. How many times as large is the cost per cup in the second move as in the first?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: First move: 10 ÷ 20 = 0.5 per cup. Second: 25 ÷ 20 = 1.25 per cup. 1.25 ÷ 0.5 = 2.5.

hints: Price each move per cup first.
Divide each move's coffee lost by its tea gained.
Divide the second price by the first.
questions.onCorrect: 2.5 times. The second move costs more per cup, which is what a bowed frontier means.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the extra coffee given up in total. The question compares the cost per cup.
That is the ratio the wrong way up. The second move is the dearer one.
